summary: Defines MIB objects for managing multicast functions independent of the specific multicast protocol in use. It obsoletes RFC 2932. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast sends one copy of a packet to many receivers. This document defines the SNMP objects that let a manager see and set up multicast on a device: which protocols run on which interface, what routes and next hops exist, which local applications have joined which groups, and which address ranges use source-specific multicast.

questions: how to monitor multicast with snmp
what is the ip multicast mib
subtitle: A protocol-independent set of SNMP objects for watching and configuring IP multicast on routers and hosts.

tldr.problem: Multicast traffic can be routed by several different protocols, and a network manager needs one set of objects that works whichever one is running, and that also covers devices which take part in multicast without routing it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IPMCAST-MIB with two scalars and eight tables, covering interfaces, routes, next hops, source-specific multicast ranges, scope boundaries and names, local listeners and scope zones.
tldr.outcome: The objects are independent of the multicast routing protocol in use, with protocol-specific objects left to other MIBs. The document obsoletes RFC 2932 and adds IPv6, per-route protocols and several new tables.

facts.label: Route table index
facts.value: Group address and prefix length, source address and prefix length

facts.label: Zone index range
facts.value: 1 to 4294967295, with zero reserved for the default zone

facts.label: Interface TTL range
facts.value: 0 to 256, where 0 forwards everything and 256 forwards nothing

today: RFC 5132 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2007. It obsoleted RFC 2932 and has not been obsoleted since. It is the standard MIB for managing IP multicast, independent of the multicast routing protocol in use.

sections.title: What the IP Multicast MIB Covers
sections.content:
The MIB describes objects used for managing IP multicast function, including IP multicast routing. The objects are independent of the specific multicast routing protocol in use; managed objects specific to particular multicast protocols are defined elsewhere.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and MIB objects are generally accessed through SNMP. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information, and the module is compliant with SMIv2, as described in STD 58. The module imports definitions normatively from other MIB modules, including HCNUM-TC, the IF-MIB, the IANA-RTPROTO-MIB, the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB, the INET-ADDRESS-MIB and the LANGTAG-TC-MIB.

The module also carries REFERENCE clauses making normative references to Administratively Scoped IP Multicast, Unicast-Prefix-based IPv6 Multicast Addresses, the IPv6 Scoped Address Architecture and the IPv6 Addressing Architecture, and informative references to several other RFCs in the text of its DESCRIPTION clauses, among them the IP-MIB, Source-Specific Multicast, PIM-SMv2, BIDIR-PIM and Tags for Identifying Languages.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the module is that it does not care which multicast routing protocol is running. A manager asks the same questions and gets the same answers whether the device speaks PIM or something else.

sections.title: How It Differs from RFC 2932
sections.content:
The document obsoletes RFC 2932, and the module it defines is a reworking of that earlier module. The changes the RFC lists are these. The module now includes support for IPv6 addressing and the IPv6 scoped address architecture, where RFC 2932 supported only IPv4. It allows several multicast protocols to perform routing on a single interface, where RFC 2932 assumed each interface supported at most one multicast routing protocol; multicast routing protocols are now per-route, as the ipMcastRouteProtocol object shows.

The module now includes objects that are not specific to multicast routing, so that multicast function can be managed on systems that do not perform routing at all, which RFC 2932 did not allow. Three tables are new: a table of Source-Specific Multicast address ranges to which SSM semantics should be applied, a table of local applications that are receiving multicast data, and a table of multicast scope zones.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version assumed IPv4 and one routing protocol per interface. This version handles IPv6, allows different protocols for different routes, and can describe a host that merely listens to multicast.

sections.title: The Eight Tables
sections.content:
The module contains two scalars and eight tables. The IP Multicast Interface Table holds multicast information specific to interfaces, and each row is indexed by the IP version and the interface index. It carries the multicast TTL threshold for the interface, so that datagrams below it are not forwarded out, a rate limit in kilobits per second for forwarded multicast traffic, and the storage type of the row. Per-interface multicast forwarding statistics are also available in the IP-MIB's ipIfStatsTable.

The IP Multicast SSM Range Table holds one row per range of multicast group addresses to which SSM semantics should be applied. The IP Multicast Route Table holds multicast routing information for IP datagrams sent by particular sources to the multicast groups known to a system, and each row is indexed by the group address and its prefix length together with the source address and its prefix length. The IP Multicast Routing Next Hop Table holds information about next hops, where each entry is one of a list of next hops on outgoing interfaces for particular sources sending to a particular multicast group address.

The IP Multicast Scope Boundary Table holds the boundaries configured for multicast scopes. The IP Multicast Scope Name Table holds human-readable names for multicast scopes. The IP Multicast Local Listener Table holds identifiers for local applications that are receiving multicast data, with entries for all addresses in the multicast range for all applications and services as they are classified on the device; each row is indexed by the group address and prefix length, the source address and prefix length, the interface index and a run index. The IP Multicast Zone Table holds an entry for each scope zone known to a system and maps each zone to the multicast address range that is the corresponding scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables cover the interface settings, the routes and their next hops, the address ranges that use source-specific multicast, the scope configuration and names, the local applications that have joined groups, and the zones that scope addresses can belong to.

sections.title: SSM Ranges, Scopes and Zones
sections.content:
The SSM range table names the ranges of multicast group addresses where Source-Specific Multicast semantics apply, so that a receiver subscribes to a group and a source rather than to a group alone. The scope tables cover administratively scoped multicast, where a scope boundary limits how far a group address may travel: the boundary table holds the boundaries configured for multicast scopes, and the scope name table holds the human-readable names for those scopes, which are writable so an operator can label them.

The zone table is about the IPv6 scoped address architecture. Each row describes a scope zone on the device and maps it to the multicast address range that is the corresponding scope. The zone index uniquely identifies a zone on a device, and each zone is for a given scope, so the scope-level information in the row is for the unique scope that corresponds to that zone. The index runs from 1 to 4294967295: zero is a special value used to request the default zone for a given scope, and zero is not a valid value for the object itself. To test whether a zone is the default zone for its scope, test whether the zone index is equal to ipMcastZoneScopeDefaultZoneIndex, the default zone index that the device will use if the default zone is requested for that scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Three separate ideas live here: which group addresses use source-specific multicast, how far a scoped group address may travel, and which local zone each of those addresses belongs to when IPv6 scoped addressing is in use.

sections.title: Compliance for Hosts and Routers
sections.content:
The module defines two compliance statements, one for a device that takes part in multicast without routing it and one for a device that routes it. The host compliance requires the local listener group and the basic group, and it states that write access is not required for ipMcastEnabled or ipMcastDeviceConfigStorageType. The router compliance requires the route protocol group, the basic group, the SSM group and the route group, again without requiring write access to those two objects.

The SSM group is optional in the host statement, and the route group is optional in the router statement, so an implementation can say which parts of the module it supports. The compliance statements also carry notes about which address types each group requires, for example that support for IPv4 or IPv6 is needed for the local listener objects and that the route group requires support for unknown and either IPv4 or IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The module says what a device has to implement to claim conformance, and it separates the case of a host that only listens from a router that forwards. Both can leave out the parts they do not use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects in the module. The RFC recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and says that deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, leaving it to the operator to configure the SNMP entity so that access is given only to principals with legitimate rights.

Several objects have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The RFC lists the effects that SET operations on the writable objects could induce: modifications to multicast routing behaviour that prevent or disrupt services provided by the network, including multicast data traffic delivery, and modifications to multicast routing behaviour that allow interception or subversion of information carried by the network. An attack could pass nominated multicast data streams through a nominated location without the sources or listeners becoming aware of the subversion. The writable objects are ipMcastEnabled, ipMcastDeviceConfigStorageType, ipMcastInterfaceTtl, ipMcastInterfaceRateLimit, ipMcastInterfaceStorageType, ipMcastSsmRangeRowStatus, ipMcastSsmRangeStorageType, ipMcastBoundaryStatus, ipMcastBoundaryStorageType, ipMcastScopeNameString, ipMcastScopeNameDefault, ipMcastScopeNameStatus and ipMcastScopeNameStorageType.

The readable objects may also be sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access and possibly to encrypt their values. GET or NOTIFY operations can reveal the topology, disposition and composition of the network, which may be commercially sensitive and may be used in preparation for attacks. They can also reveal whether multicast data is flowing in the network, or has flowed recently, and the locations of senders and recipients, which lets an attacker apply traffic analysis. The RFC notes that in some cases the information revealed by traffic analysis can be as damaging as full knowledge of the data being transported.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing these objects can break multicast or let someone intercept a stream. Reading them can reveal the shape of the network and who is sending and receiving multicast. The RFC therefore recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptography enabled.
